issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: David Chen had been forty-two when the garage door rolled shut above him, the metallic screech of its tracks still ringing in his ears when he realized he was trapped. He had come to believe that the sound of heavy doors sliding shut would always bring back the same terror he felt at that moment, a physical tightening in his chest that mirrored the weight of what was being done to him. The weeks that followed were marked by a quiet unraveling. Memories of the event would surface without warning, playing over and over in his mind like a film reel caught on the same frame. Each time the memory replayed, the terror returned to its original intensity, and alongside it, a sharp, grounding shame settled in. He felt deeply ashamed of his body, as though the trauma had left a visible mark on his skin, his posture, his very sense of physical ownership. His days as a bus driver slowly took on new contours. David spent twelve hours a day behind the wheel, but the familiar routine of his route became a landscape of thresholds. When he drove alone, the cabin felt like a sanctuary. When a fare boarded, the simple act of another person occupying his vehicle triggered a low hum of vigilance. He began to notice how easily his body grew exhausted by mid-afternoon, and he had come to believe that tiredness was not merely a sign of long shifts but a steady presence. When the fatigue set in, his guard dropped, and the auditory cues of the city-brakes hissing, turn signals clicking, the low murmur of conversation-carried the same threat they had in the garage. He adjusted his route to avoid peaks when possible, and he made sure to park between the rows of buses rather than against a wall, keeping an open line of sight. Over the months, these adjustments hardened into habits. David stopped attending the weekend team gatherings at the depot, telling his dispatcher he needed the rest, though what frightened him most was the crowded noise and the unfamiliar faces that seemed to watch him too closely. His wife, Maya, noticed how he withdrew after work. They still shared a home, but the distance between their beds grew as David began to dread the quiet moments when his body felt heavy and his mind turned inward. He had lost his faith in the idea that people generally meant well, and that mistrust settled over his interactions like a thin layer of glass. He was certain that if he let his guard down too long, he would be caught unprepared again, and his body would remain vulnerable. Now at fifty-three, David sits in a therapist's office with the morning light catching the dust motes in the air. His intake survey returned a score of seventy-six, a number that matched the texture of his days. He has not sought help until now. The accumulated weight of his fatigue, his heightened hearing, and his quiet withdrawal from his wife has simply become impossible to ignore. He is most afraid that the terror and shame will outlast his capacity to manage them, that the same sounds and the same exhaustion will continue to pull him back into that garage. What he hopes for is simpler: to drive his route without bracing for impact, to rest without feeling the world close in, and to look at his own reflection without flinching at the body that remains.
